Namespace mapping tables, overflow handling and capability inheritance rules beyond the validation outcomes shown.

findings.text: Internal helpers carry out the main work for changing real, effective, saved and filesystem user and group identities, while the corresponding system call wrappers forward their arguments to these helpers and return the helper outcome.

A session creation routine establishes a new session for the calling thread group and reports its numeric identifier, and a UTS notification routine wakes poll waiters associated with a selected UTS control entry; the setsid entry forwards to the session routine.

Group change entries accept either a real plus effective pair, a single value, or a real plus effective plus saved triple; fields holding the unchanged sentinel are left alone, other fields are validated in the caller namespace, and validation, allocation and permission problems are reported as failures.

User change entries accept either a real plus effective pair, a single value, or a real plus effective plus saved triple; sentinel-marked fields are preserved, remaining fields are validated in the caller namespace, accounting state is refreshed when the real identity changes, and validation, allocation, permission and accounting problems are reported as failures.

Filesystem-only identity entries attempt to change only the filesystem user or group value and always report the previous filesystem value, so callers cannot distinguish success from failure by return value alone and must compare the reported old value with the requested value.

Triple-query entries copy the current real, effective and saved user or group identities, translated for the caller namespace with out-of-range values replaced, into three caller-provided slots in order and stop at the first store failure.

Process and identity query entries return the caller thread-group identifier, thread identifier, parent thread-group identifier, and real and effective user and group values translated for the caller namespace; the parent query protects the parent link with read-side critical section handling.

Time accounting entries optionally fill a caller buffer with thread-group user and system time plus inherited child user and system time converted to clock units, then report elapsed wall time in clock units; a compatibility variant converts each field and the final result for the narrower clock representation.

Job-control entries move a thread-group leader to a chosen process group, query a process group or session identifier with a zero argument meaning the caller, create a new session, and report missing targets, invalid values and permission problems.

System identity entries return uname information, install a new host name after a privilege check, or copy the current host name truncated to the caller length; uname results may be altered for compatibility personalities before being handed to the caller.

A request field holding the all-ones identifier value means leave that identity unchanged and skips validation for that field, while any other requested user or group value must translate successfully in the relevant namespace or the whole request fails validation before any credential object is allocated.

Real plus effective group changes allow a real move when the target matches old real or old effective or privilege is present, and allow an effective move when the target additionally matches old saved or privilege is present; single-value group changes with privilege replace all four group values, without privilege they move only effective and filesystem values and only when the target matches old real or old saved; saved and filesystem derivation follows the new effective value under the stated conditions.

Real plus effective user changes install requested values optimistically then verify each changed field against old real, old effective, and for effective also old saved, or privilege; single-value user changes with privilege replace real and saved and refresh accounting when real moves, without privilege they succeed only when the target already equals old real or old saved; filesystem user always follows new effective user and saved follows new effective under the same conditions as groups.

Triple user and group changes return success immediately without allocating when every requested field is either unchanged or already equals the corresponding current value including the filesystem value for the effective field; otherwise any requested value that matches none of old real, old effective and old saved requires privilege, and failure is reported before allocation.

Filesystem-only changes accept the request when the target equals any of old real, old effective, old saved or old filesystem, or when the corresponding administration privilege is present; a change proceeds only when the target differs from the old filesystem value and the security hook approves, otherwise the prior value is reported without modification.

When the real user identity moves, the credential update obtains a reference-counted accounting object for the new identity, releases the old one, refreshes usage counters, and updates a per-task excess flag: the flag is left alone when counters are unchanged, otherwise it is set when the process-count usage exceeds the configured limit for a non-initial identity and cleared otherwise, deferring enforcement to a later execution stage.

User accounting objects are kept in a hash keyed by kernel user identity; allocation first looks up under protection and returns the existing entry on hit, otherwise allocates and zeroes a new entry, initializes its reference count to one, sets up optional event accounting and rate limiting, then rechecks under protection to handle races by discarding the duplicate or inserting the newcomer at the head of the bucket list.

Process-group moves default zero process and group arguments to the caller group leader and chosen process respectively, reject negative groups, require the target to exist and be a thread-group leader, allow child targets only within the same session while the child has not yet executed, allow only the caller itself otherwise, forbid moving a session leader, require a non-trivial target group to exist in the caller session, and pass a security check before changing the binding only when it differs.

Session creation fails when the caller group leader is already a session leader or when a process group already carries the numeric value of the proposed session; on success it marks the leader flag, rebinds session and group to the caller own identifier only where different, clears the controlling terminal association, and then emits connector and grouping actions outside the exclusion region while reporting the new session number.

Uname queries snapshot shared system identity under shared protection and then apply personality-dependent release rewriting and machine-field substitution before returning; host-name installation requires system-administration privilege in the owning namespace, rejects negative or over-long sizes, mixes the new bytes into device randomness, blank-pads the stored field, and notifies observers; host-name queries copy at most the caller length including termination handling.

The user-identity hash is protected by a spin lock held with interrupts disabled across each lookup and across the final recheck plus insert, while the potentially blocking allocation and initialization of a new accounting object runs without the lock.

Process-group and session changes hold the global task list in exclusive interrupt-disabled mode across target lookup, validation and rebinding, nested inside a read-side critical section for identifier structures; group and session queries and parent queries use only the read-side critical section.

Shared system-identity data is read under shared semaphore protection for uname variants and host-name queries, and mutated under exclusive semaphore protection for host-name installation, with user-memory copying performed outside the protected region.

The user accounting record observed here carries a kernel user identity, a reference count, a hash linkage node, an event-watch counter when that feature is enabled, and a rate-limit state initialized with fixed window and burst parameters plus a release-message behavior flag.

The credential record observed here carries real, effective, saved and filesystem user identities, real, effective, saved and filesystem group identities, a pointer to the owning user accounting object, a pointer to usage counters, and a pointer to the owning user namespace used for privilege checks and translations.

Time reporting uses a record with thread-group user and system fields plus inherited child user and system fields, with a narrower compatibility counterpart carrying the same four fields; system identity uses fixed-size character fields for host name and uname strings with explicit length caps and zero padding.

Credential updates follow a transaction: translate and validate requested values, allocate a new credential copy, snapshot the old credential, apply identity changes gated by privilege and equality checks, refresh accounting where required, invoke the applicable security hook, refresh usage counters for user changes, update the excess flag for user changes, then either install the new credential on success or discard it on any failure.

Accounting-object acquisition moves from protected lookup to hit return, else to unprotected allocation and initialization, then to protected recheck where a concurrent winner causes the newcomer to be torn down and the winner returned, otherwise the newcomer is linked and returned; allocation or event-setup failure yields a null result.

Process-group and session rebinding stages identifier releases in a per-call array sized by identifier type count, performs conditional changes while holding exclusion, releases exclusion, frees staged identifiers, and only for successful session creation emits follow-up connector and grouping actions.

Process-count excess during user changes does not fail the identity change but only marks the calling task for later enforcement, so callers that ignore return status may still succeed here and fail at a later execution request; filesystem-only changes and uname personality handling likewise never signal some internal failures distinctly, returning prior values or truncated data instead.

User-memory stores for triple queries, time buffers and uname or host-name transfers fail the whole call when the destination is unwritable, and credential allocation failures fail the call without modifying current identities; callers must therefore handle partial progress only as complete failure with no state change except staged flag updates described elsewhere.

The unchanged selector is the all-ones identifier value; validation failures report EINVAL, permission failures report EPERM or EACCES, missing targets report ESRCH, allocation failures report ENOMEM or EAGAIN, and bad user addresses report EFAULT; user moves gate on CAP_SETUID, group moves gate on CAP_SETGID, host-name installation gates on CAP_SYS_ADMIN; process-count enforcement consults RLIMIT_NPROC via UCOUNT_RLIMIT_NPROC with PF_NPROC_EXCEEDED marking and PF_FORKNOEXEC gating; compatibility handling consults UNAME26 and PER_LINUX32 with COMPAT_UTS_MACHINE naming; stored names honor __NEW_UTS_LEN and __OLD_UTS_LEN caps.
